Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=6 \\ y-3z &=-13 \\ -x-y-z &=-4\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array} \right]
$$



We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-6} & -24\end{array}\right].
$$



This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right]
$$



Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ -x+2y+z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ z &=2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+6z &=5 \\ y-10z &=-11 \\ 4x+8y+13z &=9\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 & 9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{11}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-2(8)=-2\,⟹\,y=-2+16=14.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=14$ and $z=8$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(14)+(8)=-3\,⟹\,x=17.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=17,y=14$, and $z=8.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨17,14,8⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ 2x+3y+2z &=14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ z &=3,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=3$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(3)=5\,⟹\,y=5-3=2.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=2$ and $z=3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(2)+(3)=6\,⟹\,x=6-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1,y=2$ and $z=3.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=0 \\ y+2z &=0 \\ x+y+3z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ x+2y+2z &=2 \\ 3x+4y+4z &=8\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ y &=5 \\ z &=-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=5$ and $z=-6$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+5+2(-6)=-3\,⟹\,x-7=-3\,⟹\,x=4.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=4,$ $y=5,$ and $z=-6.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:

\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+z &=-4 \\ 2x+5y+3z &=-10 \\ 3x+6y+4z &=-12\end{aligned}\right.

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 & -10 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & -12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & -12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=1 \\ y-3z &=-9 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-3(1)=-9\,⟹\,y=-6.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-6$ and $z=1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-(-6)+2(1)=1\,⟹\,x=-7.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-7,y=-6$, and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨-7,-6,1⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=1 \\ 2x+3y+4z &=6 \\ 3x+3y+4z &=11\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=1 \\ y &=4 \\ z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=4$ and $z=-4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(4)+2(-4)=1\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5,y=4$, and $z=-4.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨5,4,-4⟩.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ -2x+2y-3z &=-11 \\ x+z &=9.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ y-z &=1 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(5) &=1\,⟹\,y=6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(6)+2(5) &=8\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=4$, $y=6$, and $z=5.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x+6y-3z &=18 \\ -4x+8y-3z &=2 \\ y-4z &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 & 18 \\ -4 & 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 6 & -3 & 18 \\ -4 & 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ -4 & 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -22 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -22 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -22\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-6 \\ y-4z &=-3 \\ z &=-22,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=-22$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4(-22) &=-3\,⟹\,y=-91.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-91$ and $z=-22$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2(-91)+(-22) &=-6\,⟹\,x=-166.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-166$, $y=-91$, and $z=-22.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & -2 & 5 & -2 \\ 3 & 4 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y-2z &=3 \\ y+5z &=-8 \\ z &=4,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=4$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+5(4) &=-8\,⟹\,y=-28.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-28$ and $z=4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(-28)-2(4) &=3\,⟹\,x=39.\end{aligned}

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=1 \\ y-z &=-4 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(1) &=-4\,⟹\,y=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3(-3) &=1\,⟹\,x=-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-8$, $y=-3$, and $z=1.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z &=4 \\ -3x-6y+4z &=-8 \\ 3x+7y-z &=10.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z &=4 \\ y+2z &=-2 \\ z &=4,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=4$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2(4) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-10$ and $z=4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(-10)-(4) &=4\,⟹\,x=28.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=28$, $y=-10$, and $z=4.$

\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ z &=2,\end{aligned}\right.

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges

17592186049058.:topic/title: Solving 3x3 Systems of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=6 \\ y-3z &=-13 \\ -x-y-z &=-4\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array} \right]
$$



We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-6} & -24\end{array}\right].
$$



This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right]
$$



Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ -x+2y+z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ z &=2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$

$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-2(8)=-2\,⟹\,y=-2+16=14.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=14$ and $z=8$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(14)+(8)=-3\,⟹\,x=17.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=17,y=14$, and $z=8.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨17,14,8⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=6 \\ y-3z &=-13 \\ -x-y-z &=-4\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array} \right]
$$



We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-6} & -24\end{array}\right].
$$



This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right]
$$



Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ -x+2y+z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ z &=2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$

$$
x-2(14)+(8)=-3\,⟹\,x=17.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$

$$

$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-6 \\ y-4z &=-3 \\ z &=-22,\end{aligned}\right.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2(-91)+(-22) &=-6\,⟹\,x=-166.\end{aligned}

17592186096460.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
17592186096460.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$
